entry.title: Ironwood · Day 3: The Wall Closed Behind the Staff Before the Girl Was Called Off It
entry.content:
Friday 6 July 2046, morning

Tell me before you move. Don't leave it to the last minute.Scrawled on a fridge magnet note, Rowan Crescent

Natalie let herself out of the flat on Weir Street at a quarter to five and went down into the old core to walk her Friday round, into the first hard frost of the winter.

Everything had gone white in the night. The bluestone kerbs were furred with it, the cobbles in the lanes had a skin that took the print of her boots, and her breath stood in front of her face and stayed there. She had walked this round on Tuesdays and Fridays for twenty-nine years. Her feet took the corners before she did.

The first one was in the gutter at the foot of Chandler's Row, where it always came back: a grey stain on the stone the size of a dinner plate, warm enough underneath that the frost had gone off it in a ring. The itch sat faint at the back of her head. She called her staff, set the end of it on the stain and leaned, and the copper went out of her arms down the wood and into it, and it went to ash. She scuffed the ash into the crack between two stones and walked on. Four minutes.

The second was behind the bakery bins, under the downpipe, no bigger than a fist. Two minutes. A third, hardly anything, sat in the drain mouth on Bell Street. She did them the way Mum used to do the beans on the back step in Port Ellery: bent over, not looking up, moving along the row.

The grate in Salter's Lane was another thing. The itch was down in the iron. The cold had driven the blight into the bars the way it had stiffened the puddles, and when she set her staff on the grate and leaned, the copper went down the wood, stopped at the iron, and came back up her arms cold. She leaned again, harder, through her five minutes and then through five more. The frost went off the bars where the staff touched them and stayed white everywhere else.

At about the twelfth minute it bit. When she took her right hand off the staff there was a scald across the base of her palm, over the callus, a thumb wide and two thumbs long, copper-coloured, the skin gone wet and soft in the middle of the hard.

She looked at the grate. The root was still in the iron. It would sit there until a thaw loosened it, and then it would come up warm and want doing properly. She let the staff go and walked on with the hand open in the cold.

The round took her along the Tangle's wall next, the long brick side of it, with the trees standing up over the top much bigger than twenty-one years should have made them, white to the last twig. Every pole along the footpath had one of Hyejin's flyers on it, SAVE THE TANGLE over the hand-drawn vine, and the frost had got into the paper so the vines stood out stiff. The stall beside the gate had its shutter down. In its window the council's notice had curled at the corners and frozen that way. Natalie read it as she passed: PUBLIC CONSULTATION. PROPOSED SUBSTRATE HALL, EAST EDGE OF SITE. TUESDAY 10 JULY, 6.30 PM, CANAL COMMUNITY ROOMS. ALL WELCOME.

She walked a little nearer the gate than she generally did, near enough that the cold came off its bars onto her coat, and then she was past it, as she had been past it every Tuesday and Friday for twenty-one years, since there had first been a wall here to walk past.

At the corner where the lane came out on the towpath she stopped under the lamp and took Mum's letter out of her coat with her left hand.

Mum's writing had gone big and loose since the last letter, ten years back. Port Ellery at the top, underlined twice. A Tuesday in August, the fourteenth, and would Natty come home for it, and stay the week before, and be there. Natalie read the first page through. On the second, near the bottom, after a paragraph about the jetty being redone, Mum had written: So that's the 4th, love. Don't leave it to the last minute like you do.

She looked at the fourth for a while. She turned back to the first page and found the fourteenth where she had left it. She folded the letter along its old creases and put it back against the lining.

Beyond the lamp the canal was up to the lip of the towpath, skinned with ice along both edges and black and moving down the middle. The bridge stood over it white along its rail. The patch by the bridge was where it always was, and it pulled.

She meant to walk past it. She had walked past it on Tuesday.

She went down the bank on the frozen grass with her weight back on her heels. At the bottom the ice took one step and not the second, and her left boot went through into the canal. The water came over the top of the boot and up to the middle of her shin.

She stood in it. Under the bridge, set into the stonework above the waterline, the iron plate of the hatch had frost along its rim. Once the water had come to her hips in there, and she had waited with it climbing and listened. Waiting was the part she knew. She stood until her foot stopped telling her anything, and then she went back up the bank on her hands, and the scald on her palm opened on the frozen grass.

Her boot squelched for the rest of the round, and her trouser leg froze stiff from the knee down. She did the two grates past the lock, and the one in the chapel yard, and the long one under the tram stop that flooded first in any rain. At each of them she stood a moment longer than the grate needed. The chapel yard froze before anywhere else did. The tram stop one wanted doing from the kerb side, not the road. Salter's Lane wanted coming back to after a thaw, at five in the morning, by somebody who knew to feel for it in the iron. She could think of one somebody, and only one.

At twenty to seven she turned north for Kell's Lane with the frost still on her shoulders, and didn't go home to change her boot.

Isabel was in Kell's Lane by twenty to seven, on her knees on the frozen cobbles, feeling for the seam with her left fingertips before she called anything. The pesto jar was in her jacket, washed twice, the label and the glue scrubbed off, the lid screwed down. Both scalds were under chemist's gauze, the one from the culvert and yesterday's from this lane, crossing each other on the back of her right hand. Overnight they had stuck to themselves, and the hand didn't close all the way.

The static was fainter than yesterday. She had to hold her breath to hear it, a bad line behind her ear that dropped out for whole seconds, and she followed it under the fire stair and along the foot of the wall toward the downpipe, where yesterday it had nearly shouted. The frost lay over the whole lane the same, seam or no seam.

She had the order worked out from the walk over. Natalie would come in at the end of the lane and stand there. Isabel would open the wall from the downpipe end, come round under the stair, find the root and kill it, and Natalie would watch her do it. If Natalie got down on her knees under that stair, Isabel would spend the morning holding a wall for her, and she'd be back on Garnet Street's step with a jar that wasn't hers.

Mrs Vella had come out on her back step in a coat over her dressing gown, with a thermos and two chipped mugs on the step beside her. Somewhere behind the wall the little ones from number nine were hunting for puddle ice to stamp on.

"I've told them this end's mine this morning," Mrs Vella said. "Is it safe down there or isn't it? I'd like it said plain, for once."

"Ask me at eight," Isabel said.

Natalie came into the lane at seven. There was frost on her shoulders and in her hair at the parting. Her left trouser leg was dark from the knee down and stiff with it, white along the crease, and her boot left wet prints that went white behind her.

"Straight from the round," she said, before Isabel could ask where from.

"You've been in the canal."

"It's up."

So she'd walked her round and gone down to that bank again, by the bridge, and come here with it frozen up her leg, and that was the whole answer she was going to get. Isabel put it with the other things.

"I want the stair end too," she said. "I've been here since half six. I've got the line. You can watch from Mrs Vella's step."

"Stair end's mine. We said last night."

"You said. Elspeth's holding the Hundred and Fourth. If you kill the root, it's yours. She'll know. She knows everything."

"She writes whoever brings the jar. That's you."

"That's not the same and you know it's not." Isabel tried the other way in. "And you've been up since four, and you've got a foot full of ice."

"And you've a hand that doesn't close."

"It closes."

"Close it, then."

Isabel closed it. She got it most of the way, to where her nails nearly touched her palm, and the gauze over her knuckles went dark from the inside, copper-brown, spreading out to the edges. She opened it again.

Natalie didn't say anything about the gauze. "Wall's yours," she said. "All four metres. I'll be under the stair, and I'll be watching you the whole way."

Mrs Vella unscrewed the thermos and poured. Natalie took a mug and drank it standing, far too hot, the steam going up past her face. Mrs Vella held out the other.

"I'm good," Isabel said.

"You'll have one after, then."

Isabel called her staff. The pale wood came into her hands and the copper ran warm down both forearms, and the shape settled over her, and she knelt in it a moment with the staff across her knees before she put it to the wall. Her right hand wouldn't grip. She held the staff in her left and pressed the heel of the right against it, flat, which put the weight in the wrong place but put it there.

She started at the downpipe and leaned. Her copper ran out along the staff into the knit where the wall met the cobbles, and it opened under her: a line along the mortar where the frost wouldn't lie, the width of a finger, warm. She moved the staff along it a hand's width at a time and held what was behind her.

Natalie was on her knees under the fire stair with her own staff in the dark of it, turned so she could see the length of the wall. "Tell me when you're at the stair," she said.

One metre. Two. The static came up loud now, interference on every channel, all of it at the wall. Her right hand slid on the wood and she put her shoulder behind it instead. Somewhere past three metres the edges of her went. The shape thinned on her like breath going off glass, and behind her, at the downpipe, she felt the seam start to close: the first hand's width, then the next.

She could call it now. Natalie was two metres off. If she called, Natalie would come out from under the stair and lay her staff along the wall beside Isabel's, and it would be Natalie's wall as well as Natalie's root, and Isabel would carry the jar to Garnet Street for both of them.

She didn't call. She leaned harder and took the staff on another hand's width toward the stair.

"There," Natalie said, under the stair, and went in.

The root didn't wait for her. Isabel felt it go past under the wall, along the knit behind her staff, the way she'd let close, fast and low, and down. Under the stair the end Natalie had pinned went grey. At the downpipe the static dropped into the drain grate at its foot and settled there, under the block, steady.

The shape slipped off Isabel and she was on her knees on the cobbles with nothing in her hands.

The seam ran crooked and closed from the downpipe back along the wall for about a metre, and went into the drain at the foot of the downpipe. The root was under the building now, somewhere along the drain, out of reach of anything she could do from the lane.

Natalie came out from under the stair on her elbows. On the cobbles where she'd been lay a handful of grey ash, dry on the frost. Isabel's left hand went to her jacket, to the jar.

"That's not the root," Natalie said. "Leave it."

Isabel left it.

"Well?" Mrs Vella said, from the step. "It's not eight, but you've both stopped."

"No," Isabel said. "It's not safe. Keep them off the downpipe and the drain at the bottom of it, as well as the stair. It's gone into the drain under the block."

"For how long?"

"Till it's done. I don't know when that is."

Mrs Vella poured the second mug and held it out again, and this time Isabel got up and took it in her left hand. The tea was stewed and much too sweet. She drank it standing beside Natalie, with the empty jar against her ribs.

Amara Nwosu had the meter open on the kitchen table on Rowan Crescent by half past seven: the lid off, the magnifying lamp brought down from her desk and clamped to the table's edge, the soldering iron heating in its stand. The sleeve of her hoodie was pulled down over her left wrist and held there with her thumb. Mum's car was still out the front. Mum would be down by quarter to.

The needle had come off its pin at the culvert, and the pin had bent where it hit the stop. She straightened it with the small pliers under the lamp, by eye, a little at a time, faster than she should have. Then the joint. It was the one she'd thought it was: dull and grainy, the wire lifting off the pad when she touched it with the tweezers. A cold joint. She put the iron to it and fed in fresh solder, and it ran bright and smooth and set.

The needle was harder. It wouldn't sit. It dropped off the pin twice into the bottom of the box, and the second time Mum's feet were on the stairs. Amara got it back with the tweezers and pressed it on, and it went, and it sat. When she let go, it didn't fall to zero. It rested a hair above it, just shy of the first felt-tip mark, because the pin hadn't come quite straight. She tapped the box. The needle stayed where it was. So the box held together now, and whatever it read, it would read that much high. Doing the pin again meant taking the needle off, and there wasn't time. She pulled her sleeve straight.

Mum came in with her work blazer on and the Second Growth lanyard already round her neck, and a sheaf of papers under one arm. The top one said CONSULTATION EVENING, CANAL COMMUNITY ROOMS, TUESDAY 10 JULY. She put them on the bench and switched the kettle on.

"The chicken was in the sink when I got home," Mum said. "The water had gone warm."

"I forgot. Sorry. I'll do dinner tonight."

"You said you'd do it now. At twelve." Mum turned round and leaned on the bench. "So you weren't here at three. Where were you?"

"Out testing this." Amara tipped the box toward her. "It picks up interference. I wanted to see what it did away from the house."

"Away from the house where?"

"Round the crescent. The Centre."

Mum looked at her the way she looked at the news when a councillor was talking, quite still. "Your jeans are in the machine with drain lake on them to the knee," she said. "You were down at the culvert. I'm not cross about the lake. I want to know who you were with."

That was the question, and it was too late for any of the three excuses. They'd all been for the start. "On my own," Amara said.

"On your own in that water."

"It's not deep. I had boots on."

The iron ticked in its stand. Mum came over and reached for the plug at the wall. "You'll have the house down with that thing on and you looking at me." Amara reached for it too, to do it herself, and her sleeve rode up off her wrist.

Mum took her hand and turned it over under the lamp.

The scald ran from the bone on the outside of her wrist a thumb's length up her forearm, about as wide as a shoelace, the colour of a new penny, still wet down the middle.

"What's this?"

"The iron. Wednesday night."

Mum looked at the iron in its stand, and back at the wrist, and didn't let go. Her thumb stayed against the inside of Amara's arm, just under the scald, where it wasn't sore. "You burned yourself on Wednesday, and walked about in drain water on Thursday with it open, and didn't say."

"It's fine. It doesn't hurt."

"It's weeping." Mum let go and got the tin down from above the fridge, and put a dressing on it, square and white, pressing the edges flat with her fingers one side at a time. Amara held still for it. Mum had her meeting face on, the calm one, and her hands were too careful.

"Tuesday you're coming with me," Mum said.

"To the canal rooms?"

"I'm there till ten at least. I'm not having you down at that lake in the dark with your arm like this and nobody knowing where you are. You can sit at the back. Bring a book. Bring the box, if you like. There's a whole canal you can point it at."

Tuesday was meant to be the house to herself till eleven and the culvert with nobody asking. Now it was a plastic chair at the back of a room in town, an hour away, watching Mum say I hear you to people.

"Okay."

"Is that a yes? I want a yes."

"Yes."

Mum nodded, once, the way she did when a thing went in the diary. She put the papers back under her arm and drank half her tea, and kissed the top of Amara's head going past, and the front door went, and then the car.

Amara sat with the dressing on her wrist and the box in front of her. The needle still rested a hair off zero, where the pin had bent. On her phone Mum's third text from yesterday was still unanswered, and under it the three from Hyejin, still unanswered too. She opened Isabel's instead.

The box is mended. Can you come out on Sunday and watch me hold it to the grate? I'll tell you before I move.

Isabel's flat was cold when they got back to it, and Hoshi was at the corner behind the desk, yowling at the join of the two walls. When Isabel came in the cat stopped, and looked at her, and turned back to the plaster and started again.

Natalie went straight to the sink and ran the cold tap. "Hand," she said.

Isabel gave it to her. Natalie peeled the gauze back with her fingertips, a corner at a time where it had stuck. Under it the scald across her knuckles had opened along its middle when she made the fist, and the long one had wept into it where they crossed. Natalie held the whole back of the hand under the water.

It was Natalie's right hand doing the holding, palm up under Isabel's, and across the base of it, over the callus, there was a scald Isabel hadn't seen in the lane. Copper-coloured, a thumb wide, raw at the edges.

"What's that?"

"Grate in Salter's Lane. The frost had it down in the iron."

"Did you get it?"

"No. It'll keep till there's a thaw." Natalie turned Isabel's hand a little so the water ran over the knuckles. "Say the thaw comes Tuesday. Five in the morning, Salter's Lane. How do you come at it?"

"From the top, not the bottom, because the bottom's always got the bins." Isabel thought. "And it'll be in the bars, not the stone. So you feel the iron first."

"And after that?"

Natalie's left hand had gone into her coat pocket while she asked, and something in there crackled, folded paper, the same sound as yesterday on the way out the door.

It was nearly the game from when Isabel was new, five years of walking behind Natalie at dawn and being asked what came next. Only then Natalie had never asked how Isabel would come at a thing, or said a day. "The Tangle's wall. The stall gutter, if it's been raining. Then the towpath, the two past the lock, the chapel yard, which freezes first, and the long one at the tram stop, which you do from the kerb or you get your feet wet. Then home." She waited. "Why Tuesday?"

"Thaw's due Tuesday."

"That's not what I asked."

"That's all of it, though," Natalie said. "The round. You've got it all." Her hand came out of the pocket empty.

So it had been a test, and Isabel had passed it, and she couldn't tell what for. Whether a girl with a hand like hers could still be trusted with a round, probably. Her phone went in her jacket on the chair. She got it out left-handed and read it out over the tap.

"'The box is mended. Can you come out on Sunday and watch me hold it to the grate? I'll tell you before I move.'" She put it face down on the bench. "Amara. I told her that yesterday, at the culvert. Tell me before you move. It's the one thing I said that she listened to." She didn't say the rest of it: two hours there and two back, and another day with Natalie walking the old core and Kell's Lane and the bridge without her.

Natalie shut the tap off and patted Isabel's hand dry with the tea towel, round the scalds, not on them. "She's saying it, then," she said. "Somebody ought to be there to hear it."

Isabel nodded. It was the right answer, and it was the answer she'd have given herself.

"Five years you've been marking me on that round," she said. "My go. This morning. Out of ten, and the hand's not allowed in it."

Natalie looked at the hand anyway. "You stopped when it went," she said. "With a hand like that, you stopped. That's right."

"That's the hand again. And that's not a mark."

"Yeah no. It is." Natalie got clean gauze out of the chemist's bag and started winding it, round the knuckles and across the back and round the wrist, not too tight. "It's what you did right."

"So, three. Two scalds and an empty jar. My name's still never gone in the book."

Natalie looked at her. It went on a moment longer than a look needed to. Then she said, "Where's the jar?"

"Jacket."

"Keep the lid on it. She'll want it clean when you bring it."

That was all she was getting. Isabel looked at the wet trouser leg instead. "You'll freeze on the 14 like that. You don't have to. But the heater works if you kick it, and an hour on it would get you a dry sock to go home in."

"It'd want all day, that boot," Natalie said, "and my other pair's on Weir Street. Better I walk it while I can still feel the foot." She tied off the gauze and tucked the end under. Then she filled the kettle and switched it on, and got a mug down and put a teabag in it, one mug, and left it by the kettle for Isabel. She did up her coat over the wet trouser leg and went, and her boot squelched on every step of the stairs down.

The kettle came to the boil and clicked off. Isabel poured it, one-handed, and stood at the bench with it going cold, and got her phone up with her left thumb.

sunday, 10. don't go near the grate till i'm there.

She sent it. Behind the desk, at the cold corner, Hoshi drew breath and started again.

entry.title: Ironwood · Day 2: The Culvert Grate Where Amara Walked Out Ahead of the Staff
entry.content:
Thursday 5 July 2046, morning

Lost a cat near the Linden Rise culvert, grey with one white ear. Please ring before it gets dark.Handwritten notice taped to a bus shelter, Linden Rise

Natalie walked Isabel home along the river, the long way, with the water brown and high against the wall and the sky the grey of an old dishcloth. On the second-floor landing of Isabel's walk-up in the north lanes, Isabel got her key into the door and heard Hoshi before it opened.

The yowl came from the corner behind the desk. It was the same one as last night and the night before, low and long with a hitch at the end, aimed at the join of two walls where there was nothing but plaster and a curl of old tape. When Isabel came in, Hoshi stopped and looked at her. Then she turned back to the corner and started again.

"She's been doing that all week," Isabel said. "Day and night. Same corner."

Natalie stood just inside the door with her hands in her coat pockets. She didn't take the coat off.

Isabel went round the desk and put her palm flat on the plaster where Hoshi was looking. It was colder than the rest of the wall. Hoshi wound once round her ankle and yowled at her knee.

She filled the bowl, which Hoshi ignored, and put the kettle on, because the kettle was something to stand next to. Behind her she could feel Natalie looking at her, the way Natalie looked at a wall before she touched it.

She had worked out the sentence on the river path. Every blight that grew nerves went in Elspeth Hale's book on Garnet Street, with its ash in a jar, and for five years every jar of Isabel's had gone there in Natalie's hand. Last night Natalie had checked her root before she took her word for it. Every time Natalie took a thing off her she made it sound like a favour. If it was going to stop, it had to be said before Natalie could offer.

"I'm going to finish the north cut," she said to the kettle. "Tomorrow, probably. On my own."

"Okay."

That was too easy. Natalie said okay to things and then turned up anyway, at the end of the lane, with her hand out. Isabel got two mugs down. "And I'm taking the jar to Garnet Street. Me, not you. My name's never gone in the book."

Natalie looked at her. It went on a moment longer than a look needed to. Then she said, "What are you putting it in?"

"A jar?"

"Which jar."

Isabel opened the cupboard and held one up. "Pesto. It's finished."

"Wash it twice and get the label off. All of it, the glue too. She'll pick at it if you don't." Natalie took one hand out of her pocket and pointed. "And a lid that screws. Not one that clips."

"Is that a rule?"

"That's Elspeth."

The kettle clicked off. Isabel didn't pour. "So it's mine. The cut and the jar. You're not going to turn up at the end of the lane and hold your hand out."

"It's yours," Natalie said. "Both."

So there would be a step on Garnet Street, and her on it, and nobody in front of her to hand it to. Isabel poured, and slopped some, and wiped it with her sleeve.

The thing she wanted next she wasn't going to ask for. She talked about the trains instead. "It's the Kilbride line to Breen's Crossing, then a bus out to the ring road. I'll be back by four. Five, if the bus does the thing where it sits at the Centre for twenty minutes."

"Come and find me at the canal rooms when you're in," Natalie said. "Eight or so. The 14 stops outside."

"What's at the canal rooms?"

"Friends of the Tangle. I'm not going in."

"Great. Date night on the footpath outside a residents' meeting."

"There's an urn in there. I'll nick you a tea."

"Stolen tea."

"Council tea. It's not stealing, it's rates." Natalie took the mug Isabel held out and drank half of it standing, too hot, the way she always did.

She put the mug down on the desk, by Hoshi, and went. Her hand was back in her coat pocket before the door shut, holding something in there that crackled like folded paper.

Isabel ran the hot tap over the pesto jar and started on the label with her thumbnail. Behind her, in the corner, Hoshi started again.

Isabel came off the bus at the ring road just after ten, an hour out from her own lanes, and felt the ground at Linden Rise come up through her boots wrong. At home her line ran under her like her own stair in the dark. Here the pull under her feet was thin and young, laid over ten years of identical roofs, and it belonged to somebody else. It was like walking through a stranger's house with the lights off.

The drain lake was still over the path at the culvert. Amara Nwosu was waiting on the bench by the water with a box on her knees and a can from the school's vending machine going cold beside her. She was fifteen and looked it: school jacket, hood up, a satchel strap across her chest.

"Hi. You came." Amara stood. "I fixed it. The meter. Last night, at the kitchen table. It was the ground wire, and a joint, I think, so I did both."

"Cool," Isabel said, and meant it, and didn't know what else to say about a box.

Then Amara called her staff, and it was in her hands, pale green wood that smelled of sap from where Isabel stood, and the rest of her went with it. She was taller than Isabel. She looked twenty-two, twenty-three. Copper ran down both her forearms into the wood, and she stood in the wet with her weight easy on both feet, as though nothing anywhere was hurrying her and nothing ever would.

Isabel called her own. The staff came pale into her palms, the copper warm along her arms, the shape settling on her. She waded out until the water was over her ankles and the static came in at the back of her head, loud, a bad line with somebody shouting on the other end of it. It came from behind the grate where the reeds had jammed.

"Okay," Isabel said. "Stay at the edge. Two things first."

Amara stayed at the edge. Isabel was grateful for that, for about a second.

"Nerves first. If it's grown nerves, you take those off before you go anywhere near the heart."

"Why?"

"So it can't feel you coming."

"What does it do if it feels you?"

"Runs."

"Runs where?"

Isabel opened her mouth and nothing was in it. Natalie had said so it can't run, and Isabel had never asked where to. "Away. Deeper. Second thing, you never walk up on one alone."

"How close counts as alone?"

"It just. You don't do it."

"Okay." Amara nodded, once, as if she'd filed it. "But you're here. So I'm not alone." She stepped down into the water with the box held out in front of her. "Can I hold it to the grate while you watch? It's one joint. It should hold."

"Wait. I haven't told you how it goes yet."

"You told me. Nerves first, don't go alone. You're watching." She was already three steps out.

Isabel could have caught her by the sleeve. She thought of Natalie's hand closing on the staff, the coat, the key, and her own hand stayed where it was. If she grabbed this girl in front of the first thing she'd ever taught her, the girl would know Isabel didn't know what she was doing.

The needle in the box lifted. Amara took another step and it climbed past the felt-tip marks, past the last one, and hard against the stop.

Behind the grate, Isabel could see it now. A grey-brown mass the size of a car tyre was wedged into the mouth of the pipe, with the reed roots grown into its underside. Along its top edge stood a dozen pale threads, each about as long as a finger. They had all turned toward Amara.

Then the needle dropped back to nothing. Amara shook the box, and it rattled, and when she tipped it to the light Isabel could see the needle lying loose at the bottom, off its pin altogether.

The threads drew in. The mass slid back from the grate, a hand's width and then an arm's length, into the dark under the ring road, and the static went down to a mutter in the back of Isabel's skull. Where the reeds had been grown into it, their roots tore and floated up black.

Amara stood at the grate with the box against her chest. "It went higher than last time," she said. "Before it went. You saw it go higher."

"I saw," Isabel said. The water was cold through her boots. The blight was further in now than her staff could reach from the grate. Somewhere a train-line away, Natalie was doing whatever Natalie did on a Thursday without her.

Amara Nwosu stood at the culvert grate at Linden Rise with a dead box against her chest and her staff in her other hand, and the signal went behind her teeth like a held note. It hadn't gone. It had only gone back.

She had cut two on her own before this one, this winter, and told nobody, Isabel least of all. Neither of them had felt like this.

"Put that on the bank," Isabel said. "Then come back and stand where I put you."

Amara put it on the bench, upside down so the needle wouldn't fall out, and waded back. Isabel put her a body's length to the left of the grate, on the shallow side, and went in close herself, until her staff was through the bars into the dark of the pipe.

They waited. The water came to Amara's shins. Then the threads came back out of the dark, slowly, feeling along the pipe floor toward the light.

Isabel pinned the first one. Amara watched the copper run out of her arms along the pale wood and into it, and the thread go grey and still. That was nerves first. That was the rule.

Amara shifted her weight to her right foot, and the signal shifted with her.

She stood very still. The rest of the threads had turned, in the water, away from Isabel's staff and toward her. She moved her left foot a hand's width along the bank. The pressure behind her teeth slid that hand's width too. Isabel was right there with her staff in the pipe, nearer than Amara by a whole body, and they weren't looking at Isabel at all.

Nobody had said anything about that. Not Isabel, not the forums.

"They're following me," Amara said. "Not you."

Isabel's head came round. "That's not. They feel whoever's closest."

"You're closest."

Isabel didn't answer that. Her hands were shaking on the staff. Amara could see it from where she stood, the end of the wood ticking against the bars.

"Okay but what if I walk, along the bank, really slowly, and they come out after me, and you take them as they come? Is that a dumb idea? It might be a dumb idea."

"Natalie never said anything about doing it like that."

"Is it wrong, though?"

Isabel breathed out through her mouth. "Go slow."

Amara went slow. The threads came out of the pipe after her, one by one, into the grey light at the grate's edge, and Isabel took them one by one as they cleared the bars. Four. Seven. Ten. Her copper was the inside of a two-pence piece held to a lamp, and Amara felt her own arms warm in answer every time Isabel leaned.

The last one whipped. It came off the grate in a flick and went along the water to Amara's staff, and up it, and over her wrist. On its way back it went across the back of Isabel's hand where she gripped the bars.

It went grey under Isabel's staff a second later. The signal dropped to a single low note, far in under the road.

Amara looked at her wrist. A scald ran from the bone at the outside of it a thumb's length up her forearm, along her copper, about as wide as a shoelace, the colour of a new penny, wet. Across Isabel's raw knuckles ran a shorter one, the same colour, already weeping.

"The heart's under the road," Isabel said. "I can't reach it from here, and I'm not going in there. Without the nerves it can't feel us. It'll keep."

Amara wanted to ask how long keep was, and didn't. Isabel waded out of the water, slowly, and looked at her, and not at her wrist.

"Where'd you learn to stand like that?"

Amara had excuses ready, three of them, and every one was for the start of a thing. It was too late for any of them now. She looked at the water. "I read a lot," she said. "On the forums." It came out small.

"You didn't read your feet." Isabel looked at her a moment more. "You've stood at one of these before."

Amara didn't say yes. She didn't say no either, and Isabel nodded slowly, as though not saying no was an answer, and it was. So Isabel knew. Not the two, not where, but that her feet had done this before, and now every time Amara asked her something Isabel would be wondering what she already knew.

"Next time, tell me before you move," Isabel said. "Not after. Before."

That was all. Not that was right. Amara nodded and let the staff go, and her shape went with it, and the cold came straight through her school jacket. She was looking up at Isabel now, not down.

Isabel stayed as she was a while after, staff across her knees on the bench, copper still running faint down her arms. Then she let it go too.

"You're taller than me in it," Isabel said.

"I'm still growing, though," Amara said. "Out of it, I mean. I've gone through two pairs of school shoes this year. So I'll catch you up anyway."

Isabel said her bus went at the half hour.

Amara's phone went three times in her pocket. Mum texted in threes, and the third was always the question. Mum was at work till six.

Did you have lunch?

Chicken's defrosting in the sink, put it in the fridge by three please.

Where are you today?

Yes, I had a sandwich.

I'll do it now.

She left the third. Under it, further down the screen, sat three messages from a girl called Hyejin, who had written to her the night she posted: what it costs, how girls die, that nobody is coming. She had read them twice each. She hadn't answered those either.

She pulled her sleeve down over her wrist before Isabel could look at it.

Elspeth Hale opened the door of her house on Garnet Street before Natalie had knocked twice, and looked past her, down the step, to see who wasn't on it.

"Just me," Natalie said.

"So I see." Elspeth was in a cardigan nobody had made since Natalie was at school, and a skirt older than the cardigan. She looked seventeen. She had looked seventeen when Natalie first stood on this step, and when Natalie's mother was a girl. She stood back to let her in.

The front room was as it always was. The ledger lay open on the table, the last line in grey-brown ink: The Hundred and Third: Sagittaria. Beside it sat the ink stone, wiped and dry, and the steel nib on its rest, and a row of clean jars with nothing in them.

"I've had the stone out since Tuesday night," Elspeth said. "You posted it done."

"I posted the nerves done. The north cut's still open."

"Then I've had the stone out two days for half a job."

"A bit longer, then. Iz is closing it tomorrow. The jar's hers to bring."

Elspeth sat, and folded her hands on her knees. Natalie stayed standing. "I've never had her at my door."

"You will. I want you to wait for her." Natalie put her hand in her coat pocket and kept it there, off the letter, which was folded in three against the lining. "And if I turn up with that jar, send me home with it."

Elspeth's eyebrows went up a fraction. "That isn't how it's done. Whoever brings the ash."

"Then see that it's her that brings it."

Elspeth looked at the empty jars. "And when she's brought it," she said, "and I've written her, who does she bring the next one to, after me?"

"Not me."

"You've a steady hand. You know every girl in the Bay by her walk."

"I said no at Easter. It's still no."

"So you've said."

Natalie heard it land nowhere. She had heard it land nowhere at Easter, too. Elspeth's shoulders hadn't moved at all.

"My edges haven't been walked in a fortnight," Elspeth said. "Not by me. I know who's been walking them." She didn't say who, and Natalie didn't ask.

There was the itch, faint, somewhere off toward Hollis Street. Nothing much. Not hers. Natalie thought of the old core at dawn tomorrow, the grates and the lanes and the five-minute cuts, and of it some other morning with nobody on it at all, and only one somebody she could think of to put there.

"And how's your friend?" Elspeth asked, with the weight on friend.

"Teaching. Out at Linden Rise."

"The new growth." Elspeth never learned the names out there. "There's a girl out there three weeks found who hasn't come to me."

"That's the one Iz is teaching."

"Is it." Elspeth looked at her for a while, the long patient look she gave everything, as though it were a matter for the record. Then she got up, closed the ledger on its ribbon, and set the nib straight on its rest. "I'll hold the Hundred and Fourth. I'll not write it for anybody else, and I'll not take that jar from your hand. Tell her the step's here."

"I'll tell her."

At the door Elspeth said, "Mind the canal on your way. It's up."

"I know," Natalie said, and went down the step with her hand still in her pocket.

Isabel came back into the north lanes late in the afternoon and went straight to Kell's Lane without going home first, because if she went home first she'd sit down.

The lane looked as it always did: stacked windows, the fire stair down one side, a pram somebody had left under it. The static was faint. She had to stand still in the middle of the cobbles for a full minute before she found it, a thin bad line behind her ear that kept dropping out. On Tuesday night she'd walked off this cut half done and the opening had been right there under her heel. It wasn't there now.

She called her staff. Her arms complained, after the culvert. She laid the pale wood along the cobbles where she'd left the seam and felt for it.

It had closed over. Not straight, the way she'd opened it, but crooked, knitting back on itself across the lane and then off sideways, under the fire stair, toward the foot of the block wall. She followed it with the staff end, a step at a time, losing it and finding it.

"You'll catch your death, down there on your knees."

Mrs Vella had come out onto her back step, which gave onto Kell's Lane, with a basket of washing on her hip. She'd been on Linnet Lane forty years and she knew who was in and who was out and who wasn't eating, and she treated all of it as her business.

"I'm good," Isabel said. "Dropped something."

"It's been cold in this lane since Tuesday night. Colder than the weather. I said so this morning to anyone who'd listen." Mrs Vella pegged out a pillowcase. "The little ones from number nine play down that end. Should I be keeping them off?"

Isabel didn't answer yet. She'd lost the seam at the bottom step of the fire stair. To find where it really went she had to push into it, and she knew that, and she did it: leaned, and let the copper run out along the staff into the knit.

The seam pushed back. It came up the staff the way the thread had come up Amara's that morning and went over the back of her hand, over the scald she already had from the culvert. When she looked, the new one ran from the second knuckle to the wrist bone, as wide as a pencil, copper-coloured and wet, crossing the first.

She swore at it, quietly.

But she had it now. The true line went under the fire stair, along the foot of the wall for about four metres, and stopped at the downpipe. All of it would have to be opened again along its length and held while she went for the root. On Tuesday night it would have been ten minutes. Now it was an hour, maybe more, and all of it holding.

She could start now. It was light for another two hours. She had nothing left in her arms after the culvert, and she could feel the shape thin at her edges already, the way it went before it slipped. She held it anyway, a moment longer, crouched by the downpipe, before she let it go.

Tomorrow. After Natalie's round. She didn't look at why that was the time she'd picked.

"Keep them off the stair end," she said. "Just till tomorrow. The cobbles are lifting."

"The cobbles have been lifting since nineteen-ninety." Mrs Vella looked at her hand. Isabel put it in her pocket. "Come in and have a cup of tea. I've the kettle on and nobody to drink it."

"I've got to be somewhere at eight."

"It's half five."

"I've got to feed the cat."

"That cat," Mrs Vella said, "has been shouting at the wall since breakfast. I could hear it from the yard." She held the back door open with her hip and waited, with the empty basket, and did not go in.

Natalie was outside the community rooms by the canal when Iz came in on the 14, a little after eight. Behind the glass the Friends of the Tangle had the lights on and the stacking chairs out in rows, and somebody was standing at the front with a sheet of paper. Every pole on the street wore one of Hyejin Park's flyers, SAVE THE TANGLE over a hand-drawn vine, some of them three deep. Natalie had walked past twenty-one years of Hyejin and never once asked her anything. Down the line at the Exchange the Back Room was on, and she wasn't going to that either.

The canal was high from last night, black and quick against the brick. A little way along, past the lock, the patch by the bridge sat where it always sat, and pulled.

Iz came off the tram with her hand in her jacket pocket and her shoulders up round her ears. She hadn't slept much, and she'd used herself up somewhere today. Natalie didn't say so.

"No tea," Natalie said. "They've got a woman guarding the urn."

"Council security. Figures."

They stood under the pole. Iz told it in order, the way she told everything: the bus, the drain over the path, the girl on the bench, the box that went to the stop and then dropped its needle. The threads that turned. The girl walking the bank so they'd come out after her. The heart under the ring road. Natalie listened and looked at the water past the lock, and made herself look back.

"They followed her," Iz said. "Not me. I was closer. You never said anything about that."

"No."

"Is that a thing?"

"Not one I've seen." Which was true, and narrower than the question.

"And Kell's Lane's knitted over crooked. It goes under the fire stair and along the wall to the downpipe. It's an hour now, holding the whole way." Iz stopped. Her eyes had gone past Natalie's shoulder, toward the bridge, and come back. "You keep looking at the bridge."

"Water's up."

Iz waited, and when nothing else came she let it go, and Natalie watched her decide to.

"So tomorrow," Iz said. "After your round. I want you there. Watching. Not doing anything. Just there."

The itch was faint and far off and nothing to do with this. Natalie thought of a wall four metres long and Iz holding it open alone with nothing in her arms, and threads that went for the wrong girl.

"I'll come straight to Kell's Lane from the round," she said. "Seven, about."

"And watch."

"I'll take the stair end. You do the rest."

Iz held up her hand under the streetlight. There were two scalds across the back of it, crossing, both weeping. "You said it was mine. This morning, you said both."

"The jar's yours. I've told Elspeth. She won't take it off me if I turn up with it. She'll hold it for you."

"That's not what I asked."

"I know."

"So you'll watch me do three metres of it and then you'll do the bit that's hard."

"I'll do the bit under the stair, where you can't see the root." Natalie could hear herself, and couldn't make herself say the other thing. "Iz. Look at your hand."

Iz put it back in her pocket. Her shoulders came down, not the way they had this morning in the kitchen. "Seven, then."

"Seven."

The door of the rooms banged open behind them, and a man in a fleece came out with a roll of tape and a fresh stack of flyers. He taped one to the pole beside Natalie's head, over the old ones, and smoothed the vine flat with his thumb. The 14 came back round the other way, and Iz got on it without looking back. Natalie walked home by Weir Street, not the towpath, past a flyer on every pole.

entry.title: Ironwood · Day 1: The Answer Given in Daylight on the Canal Bank
entry.content:
Wednesday 4 July 2046, morning

DO NOT USE THE TOWPATH AFTER HEAVY RAIN.Council notice, cable-tied to the railing of the old canal bridge

Amara Nwosu stood ankle-deep where the night's rain had pushed the drain lake over the path, at the culvert under the ring road at Linden Rise. Water still ran off the concrete above her in cold strings. The reeds along the lake had jammed against the grate in the night, and where they met the water they had gone black at the root.

The signal sat behind her teeth and at the back of her head. That was how the blight felt to her: a pressure that got stronger the closer she came. It was strong now.

In both hands she held the meter, a box of her own wiring, the dial marked in felt-tip at midnight and the needle loose on its pin. It was meant to read what her head read. She had run out of time before the ground wire, and one end hung bare inside.

She wanted to see it work. She wanted to show it to Isabel, the girl who had replied to her post. Isabel would be impressed, right? And then she'd be able to learn how to cut cleanly, and what worked and what didn't, and she'd be good at it. Especially with this blight, whose pressure was nothing like the two she'd cut before. Sharper, like a migraine. She moved, and she almost felt something move with her. Was it watching her?

She turned toward the grate. The needle stirred, twitching. Did that count? She held the box out at arm's length, stretching, trying to be close to and far from the grate at the same time. The needle lifted, climbed, and then dropped completely. As she pulled it back, it stayed dead.

She shook the box. Nothing, just a slight rattle. She didn't have her screwdriver here, but she could already tell it was wire banging around. Probably a cold solder joint.

So the box worked, or near enough. She felt her grin coming through, and tamped it down. Be professional.

She checked her phone again. No response from Isabel. She waited, tapping her foot, and then the drizzle found the gap at her collar and she checked again.

She could go nearer, and find out what this blight did with someone standing that close to it. Or she could stay where she was, in water to the ankle, and wait for the girl who wasn't there, and might not show up at all. The forums said a girl didn't walk up on one that might have nerves, not alone.

She stayed. The cold came through her boots and into her toes. She counted to ten between checks, caught herself at it, and made a face. God, she was such a kid.

Still, nothing. She waited.

Isabel woke in Natalie's flat, expecting to find a weight behind her back and feeling nothing instead. The sheet on Natalie's side was cold, and when Isabel got up, she noticed the coat gone from its hook by the door. The mugs from last night were up on the bench, beside the sink. The keys weren't in the dish. Natalie had them, then. Probably.

She stood and looked at the couch for a moment too long. Last night Natalie had told her about the ditch under the old canal bridge, and stopped halfway through, and Isabel did not have to think about where to look. She dressed quickly, grabbed her phone, and left the flat.

She went out along the towpath, the damp of yesterday's jacket chilling her. The canal had come over the path in places and the mud squelched around her boots. The old bridge came up out of the drizzle, and below it, halfway down the bank on the wet grass, Natalie was going carefully toward the black water. She hadn't looked up yet.

Isabel stood for a moment, weighing. If she stayed here, Natalie would keep going. If she called out, Natalie might stop. But then they'd have to talk.

"Natalie."

Natalie stopped. For a moment she stood as she was, one foot lower than the other on the slope. Then she turned and came back up, and stood on the path next to Isabel, close but not.

Isabel made herself look at her face. "What are you doing out here?"

Natalie turned and looked back at the flood-swelled canal running past. Water ran off her hair and down her jaw, and she didn't wipe it. There was something in the way her eyes stared, Isabel thought, but she couldn't describe it. As the moment stretched, she gave it up. "You don't have to tell me. Sorry."

"It's okay. It's not something I'm ready to talk about just yet. You'll have to be patient with me on that. Okay?"

"Okay." A beat, and her stomach grumbled, which set off a small giggle from Natalie, and then the two were laughing, breath fogging in the air.

"Come on, let's go back to mine," Natalie said. "I'll do eggs. Proper ones."

They went up past the bridge, where a council notice had been cable-tied to the railing, laminated, gone cloudy with rain. DO NOT USE THE TOWPATH AFTER HEAVY RAIN. Natalie read it out, flat as a newsreader, and looked down at the water over both their boots.

"Bit late," Isabel said, with a smile. "Did you take the keys? I didn't lock up. I couldn't find them."

Natalie patted her coat pocket, and it jangled. "Always."

"Okay. Good." Isabel looked ahead along the towpath, where it went under again past the lock. "We should cut up by the garages. It'll be drier."

"You've thought about this."

"I try," Isabel demurred. Natalie made a small sound that might have been a laugh, and let her lead.

It was always easier to talk to Natalie, and she wanted to figure out why, but maybe not this morning. Not after how hard it had been last night. This morning, she would just enjoy it. Or try to.

She felt a buzz in her pocket, the girl from the forums. Right. She tapped out a quick reply, tossed the phone back in her pocket, and looked up as Natalie asked "Who's that?"

"The girl from the forums. She wants me to teach her."

Natalie didn't say anything for a few steps. "You going to?"

"Someone has to." Left unsaid was whether she could. Isabel knew she could. It didn't need saying.

The silence grew legs and shadowed them. As they stopped at the next traffic light, something simmered in her, and a question burst out.

"I need to know. Was last night real? To you?"

A breath, and then another. "It's real," Natalie said.

Isabel shifted, her hands unclenched. Then she looked for the rest of it in Natalie's face, the catch or the lie or anything at all, and found the calm Natalie wore on a cut, and nothing past it.

Then why leave? Why the bridge? Next time she would be up before the coat left the hook.

At the grate, Amara went to message Isabel again.

Can you show me how to cut today? I've done two already, but this one's different.

She backspaced the second part out, and tapped send. If Isabel knew, she might say no, she might think Amara was getting ahead of herself.

This time the answer came inside a minute.

sure. when do you want to meet? after 10

Amara replied with a time and place before she could think, and retreated to a bench, phone in her pocket. It was damp, and she sat anyway. Not like she was getting any drier today.

She pulled out the box again, turned it over in her hands. She had been excited to show it to Isabel; barely started and already she was doing things that no one else had done. But now she had no proof. She tossed it back in her satchel.

She ran through the questions she wanted to ask. She wanted to be sophisticated, didn't want to be asking beginner questions. "How often do you walk your rounds?" she asked the air. Or, perhaps, one from the forum, "How long do you give a root before you call it dead?" No one was around to hear her pondering, it was a miserable day to be outside. "How close can you get before it notices you?" Nah, too basic.

A yawn forced its way out of her tight jaw, and Amara remembered that vending machine outside the school. She meandered over and grabbed a can of hot coffee, making a noise at the bitter taste. At least it was something warm to hold, and eventually she'd get used to it, she supposed.

She wandered back to the bench to wait, hands warm and eyes open.
